title: What this week’s cyber chaos revealed about what’s coming for the 'Digital Grid’
summary: Here's how AI hacking, data breaches, and massive outages have wreaked havoc on critical infrastructure, and what to expect moving forward – including shopping safely this holiday season.
body_markdown:
If it felt like half the internet was having a bad week, you weren't imagining it. Over the span of just a few days, Americans watched major technology outages disrupt air travel, ticket sales, workplaces, and their phones. Chances are another data breach or outage will be announced by the time you finish reading this story. To top it all off, hackers published stolen data allegedly connected to customers of major financial companies.


Though U.S. officials as well as[Gen’s cybersecurity experts](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/insights/leadership-perspectives/the-digital-grid) have stated there is no evidence that the recent wave of outages was the result of a coordinated cyberattack, the resulting panic sent many Americans into doomsday mode.


For instance, consumer anxiety helped fuel a run on emergency-preparedness products at Costco.[MoneyLion reported](https://www.moneylion.com/trending/money/tech-outages-drive-costco-surge-emergency-prep) that 21 of Costco's 26 high-ticket online generators had sold out online amid increased demand, while consumers also stocked up on bulk essentials. Fear itself can lead to disruption.


Taken together, the events illustrated something bigger about this moment in cybersecurity: Like a power grid,[our “Digital Grid” is extremely interconnected](https://lifelock.norton.com/learn/internet-security/digital-grid-vulnerabilities) , and attackers are increasingly using our own heightened emotions alongside AI tools capable of probing those technical connections faster than most humans could hope to intervene.


## Third-party attacks left the internet in a standstill all week long


Whether it was an outage with tools you use at your job or an attack putting your accounts at risk, the bottom line is that stuff wasn’t working, and it seemed like your personal information was potentially in danger.


For example, consider that attackers injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely Web projects used by 178 of the world's biggest brands such as BBC, CNN, Zoom, Ikea, and Equifax. Because the malicious software was delivered through a trusted infrastructure, visitors could load it while visiting otherwise legitimate websites.


Meanwhile, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that customer email addresses and names were leaked by attackers targeting third-party service providers rather than the bank itself. Visa also faced a cyber incident involving a third party in the Asia-Pacific region, resulting in the exposure of customer data. (However,[Visa](https://cybernews.com/security/visa-card-data-breach/) said payment data and card numbers were not affected.) Mastercard similarly confirmed that an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited amount of non-payment information associated with some customers enrolled in a benefit program.


These are all textbook problems with our brittle Digital Grid: Attackers don't necessarily have to compromise hundreds of companies individually. They just need to compromise technology those companies already trust. Marketing platforms, loyalty programs, cloud providers, analytics services, and website tools are all woven together in a tapestry of customer information.


What connects this week's incidents isn't necessarily the company whose logo is on your credit card: It’s the ecosystem of vendors behind that company. That means one compromised supplier can potentially create a doorway to many recognizable brands.


### Then there were the outages that seemed never-ending


At roughly the same time, Americans watched a 10-day series of technology problems affect services ranging from Microsoft Outlook to federal agencies and a ground stop that hit every airline in America. Officials stated investigations had not yet found evidence tying the disruptions together as a coordinated malicious campaign.


However, here's[where cybersecurity and infrastructure resilience](https://www.avast.com/c-digital-grid-and-november-outages) collide. An outage doesn't have to be caused by hackers to demonstrate what a successful cyberattack might look like when it does happen. Take away email, payments, transportation, or communications long enough, and disruption to the Digital Grid starts becoming disruption to the physical world.


## Cyberthreats during holiday shopping: How vulnerable infrastructure creates the perfect environment for scams


These events taking place during what is typically the busiest shopping season of the year make this pretty impeccable timing for cybercriminals. Tech outages not only cause people to panic-buy at stores like Costco but also make it easy to click the wrong link when consumers are already bombarded with shipping notifications, password-reset requests, promotional emails, and payment messages.


More serious cases, like a breach that reveals your name, phone number, email address, travel plans or loyalty program activity, may not immediately drain your bank account, but that information can become raw material for another attack. These scams or phishing expeditions become much harder to recognize when criminals know which company you actually use, your name, recent travel activity, or other details. That makes an important rule even more important: Don't treat familiarity as proof of authenticity.


Think about how many Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or Christmas shopping emails you are getting right now, then add genuine news about payment-company breaches and widespread outages. It’s a recipe for chaos, which can result in an unusually convincing cover story for scams.


Urgency has always been one of the scammers' favorite weapons. AI can make the message wrapped around that urgency much more convincing. Here are a few key takeaways about messages you should be especially skeptical of before clicking or claiming:


- A holiday order couldn't be delivered because of an outage.
- A credit card must be "reverified" following a breach.
- A retailer needs updated payment information.
- A bank account has temporarily been frozen.
- A purchase needs to be confirmed immediately.
- A package requires an additional delivery fee.
- An emergency shortage requires buying something immediately.


If you receive an urgent shopping, banking, or account-security message, don't use the link or phone number provided in the message. Open the company's official app, type its website into your browser yourself, or call the number printed on your physical card.


## AI changes the speed of cybercrime


AI makes this already-precarious environment more consequential. Generative AI can potentially help criminals turn stolen information into personalized phishing emails, realistic customer-service conversations, translated scam campaigns, and voice impersonation at an enormous scale. And the FBI this week warned of autonomous AI attacks.


According to reporting on this threat, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework called ARTEX can perform reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, exploit systems, escalate privileges, and steal data with limited human involvement as quickly as under three hours.


Other research suggests this isn't an isolated development. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant recently observed attackers using AI frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop, including an experimental system that could examine software changes after a patch, identify the vulnerability, and generate an exploit.


That doesn't mean AI has suddenly invented completely new forms of cybercrime. Rather, AI has accelerated familiar threats such as phishing, supply-chain attacks, and extortion. Fully autonomous attacks remain comparatively rare for now. The more realistic concern is that AI doesn't need to invent a revolutionary cyberweapon to be dangerous. It can make existing scams faster, cheaper, more personalized, and easier to scale.


## Trusting the Digital Grid: Why critical infrastructure is the bigger concern and what to expect next


Perhaps the most important cybersecurity story isn't any individual breach, because if one cloud provider, software update, vendor, or communications network fails, how many other services fail with it? This week's outages provided a stress test to show how quickly uncertainty can spread from computer screens into airports, banks, and even shopping carts.


The future is potentially messier than one AI hacker taking down the internet. However, you can probably expect more automated vulnerability hunting, more attacks against third-party providers, more stolen data being fed into sophisticated phishing campaigns, and shorter windows between discovering a security flaw and seeing attackers try to exploit it.


To help you stay vigilant and avoid some financial shocks, here are some ways to stay prepared:


- **Turn on multi-factor authentication.** Use a passkey or authenticator app where available rather than relying exclusively on SMS.
- **Keep devices updated.** The Optimizely incident specifically demonstrated why outdated devices can create additional exposure.
- **Slow down when a message creates urgency.** An alleged outage or breach is a reason to verify independently, not click faster.
- **Monitor financial accounts.** Check unfamiliar transactions and set alerts for charges and account changes.
- **Use unique passwords.** A password manager makes this significantly easier.
- **Go directly to the source.** If your bank, airline or retailer supposedly needs something from you, contact it independently rather than responding to an unsolicited message.


Perhaps most importantly, don't panic. Cybercriminals benefit when people are scared, rushed, or confused. This week's generator-buying surge demonstrates how quickly concerns about technology can influence real-world behavior.


Ultimately, modern cybersecurity depends on the chains of trust. Trust in your bank, trust in the websites you give your credit card information to, and trust in payment companies in general. Attackers don't always need to break just one of those links to cause a huge disruption in all the trust you have in the Digital Grid.


That's the real takeaway from this extraordinary week in cybersecurity. Make sure you have the protection you need.
